record.title: Collage Poetry Exhibition Donation Drive
record.description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. What is Collage Poetry? Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. record.title: Holocaust Memory and its Discontents: The Case of Germany, Featuring Michael Rothberg
record.description: In this lecture, Rothberg will trace the rise of what became known as the “German model” of addressing a nation’s own crimes. While a few years ago it seemed obvious that countries like the United States could “learn from the Germans” to confront their troubled pasts (in Susan Neiman’s terms), today the situation seems more complicated. Focusing especially on the Federal Republic of Germany, Rothberg will survey state-level engagements with National Socialism and the Holocaust as well as grassroots efforts at commemoration that began in the 1980s. He will show how the model of Vergangenheitsbewältigung (“coming to terms with” or “mastering” the past) was consolidated after German unification and then started to fray in the twenty-first century. He will conclude by emphasizing how migration, colonialism, and the October 7/Gaza moment intersect with — and have come to unsettle — German Holocaust memory. This event is generously sponsored by July Galper. How to Attend This event is offered both in person at Geisel Library and virtually via Zoom beginning at 5 p.m. Pacific time. Click the Register button at the top of this page and select your preferred mode of attendance. About the Speaker Michael Rothberg is the 1939 Society Samuel Goetz Chair in Holocaust Studies and Professor of English and Comparative Literature at the University of California, Los Angeles. His research focuses on the social and cultural implications of political violence and its afterlives, and his writings have been translated into French, German, Hindi, Hungarian, Italian, Japanese, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Swedish, and Turkish. His books include “The Implicated Subject: Beyond Victims and Perpetrators” (2019), “Multidirectional Memory: Remembering the Holocaust in the Age of Decolonization” (2009), “The Holocaust: Theoretical Readings” (2003; co-edited with Neil Levi), and “Traumatic Realism: The Demands of Holocaust Representation” (2000). With Yasemin Yildiz, he is completing “Memory Citizenship: Migrant Archives of Holocaust Remembrance.” He has also written for public-facing venues such as Inside Higher Ed, Los Angeles Review of Books, the Los Angeles Times, and The Nation, as well as German-language publications such as Die Zeit, Berliner Zeitung, and Geschichte der Gegenwart. The 2021 German translation of “Multidirectional Memory” prompted a national debate in the mainstream press about the relationship between the Holocaust and colonialism. His forthcoming book, “The Holocaust Analogy: On the Use and Misuse of Historical Comparison” (2027), grows out of that experience and considers contentious public debates about the use of Holocaust comparisons. About the Series The Holocaust Living History Workshop (HLHW) series is an education and outreach program co-sponsored by the UC San Diego Library and the Jewish Studies Program. It aims to preserve the memories of the victims and survivors of the Holocaust by offering public events involving witnesses, descendants and scholars and through the use of the USC Shoah Foundation Institute’s Visual History Archive. Past HLHW workshops are now part of the Library’s digital collections and are available online.

record.title: Film Screening: "Let the City Speak"
record.description: Join us for a screening of Let the City Speak, a documentary following Quetzal, the GRAMMY-winning Chicano rock band that emerged from East Los Angeles’ vibrant music and arts scene in the mid-1990s. Led by Quetzal Flores and Martha Gonzalez, the band found inspiration in the mountains of Chiapas, Mexico, embracing a philosophy that would shape their music, community organizing, and grassroots activism for decades. Directed by Emmy Award-winning filmmaker Akira Boch, who has documented the band for nearly 30 years, the film explores the enduring connections between music, cultural identity, social justice, and community. It celebrates the Zapatista spirit that continues to guide the band’s artistic and activist work. Following the screening, attendees will have the opportunity to engage with Quetzal Flores, GRAMMY-winning producer, composer, musician, and cultural organizer, and Akira Boch, Emmy Award-winning filmmaker and former director of the Watase Media Arts Center at the Japanese American National Museum. Through music, activism, and storytelling, Let the City Speak invites audiences to consider how artists can define success on their own terms and use their creative work to inspire meaningful change. Featured Guests Quetzal Flores is a GRAMMY-winning producer, composer, musician, and cultural organizer from East Los Angeles. He founded and directs Quetzal, an influential and critically acclaimed band known for its powerful blend of music, community engagement, and activism. Akira Boch is an Emmy Award-winning filmmaker and former director of the Watase Media Arts Center at the Japanese American National Museum. A graduate of UCLA’s Film Directing program, his work explores historical memory, diasporic identity, and contemporary culture. Event Co-Sponsors: Suraj Israni Center for Cinematic Arts, Muir College Office of the Provost and the Department of Theatre & Dance

record.title: Understanding Love and Eros in the Holocaust: A German-Jewish Gay Romance in Prague, Featuring Anna Hájková
record.description: Where are the stories of great queer love in the Shoah? There are almost none. Anna Hájková explains why the history of same-sex desire in the Shoah, that is, queerness among Jews persecuted by the Nazis for their race, has been excluded and marginalized, and how its return to our understanding of the Holocaust can offer an inclusive and feminist history of this genocide. Based on original and extensive archival research, her talk offers an introduction into the queer history of the Holocaust for beginners and advanced alike. Please note, this talk will include discussion of sexual/ized violence. This event is the Lou Dunst Memorial Lecture. How to Attend This event is offered both in person at Geisel Library and virtually via Zoom beginning at 5 p.m. Pacific time. Click the Register button at the top of this page and select your preferred mode of attendance. About the Speaker Anna Hájková is Reader for modern European continental history at the University of Warwick in the United Kingdom, where she co-directs the Centre for Global Jewish Studies. Her first book, “The Last Ghetto: An Everyday History of Theresienstadt,” was published in 2020. Hájková’s second book, “People Without History are Dust: Queer Desire in the Holocaust” (2025), was awarded the National Jewish Book Award 2026. She is a pioneer of queer Holocaust history, and her work was awarded the Orfeo Iris Prize in 2020. About the Series The Holocaust Living History Workshop (HLHW) series is an education and outreach program co-sponsored by the UC San Diego Library and the Jewish Studies Program. It aims to preserve the memories of the victims and survivors of the Holocaust by offering public events involving witnesses, descendants and scholars and through the use of the USC Shoah Foundation Institute’s Visual History Archive. Past HLHW workshops are now part of the Library’s digital collections and are available online. Photo Credit: Václav Jirásek

record.title: UC GIS Week Map-a-thon
record.description: Join the Library for a Map-a-thon as part of the UC GIS Week. We will contribute to the Missing Maps project, which empowers volunteers to map vulnerable areas, assisting humanitarian organizations trying to meet the needs of people who live at risk of disasters and crises. Each year, disasters around the world affect or displace 200 million people. Many of the places where these disasters occur are literally ‘missing’ from open and accessible maps and first responders lack the information to make valuable decisions regarding relief efforts. We’ll trace buildings and roads from satellite images—no experience is required! Your contributions will support critical recovery efforts in crisis-prone regions. Join us for the whole event or drop in as your schedule allows. This is also a fun and meaningful way to de-stress. No experience or special skills are required. This is a Bring Your Own Device event, so bring your own laptops and chargers. Tell us you’re coming by registering today! record.description: Free Public Forum Wildfires are one of the greatest societal challenges of the 2lst century, but our solutions aren't working. The Philosophy of Science Association (PSA) Public Forum invites you to join experts Alexandra Syphard and Richard Halsey for an interactive conversation on the philosophical challenges surrounding the complexity of wildfires. record.title: New Writing Series: PhD Creative-Critical Poet Reading
record.description: About New Writing Series UC San Diego’s New Writing Series invites local, national, and international authors to read and perform throughout the academic year. Welcoming a wide range of authors and genres, including playwrights, poets, translators, essayists, critics, fiction writers, and performance artists, the New Writing Series celebrates both emerging and established award-winning writers. Readers also include Department of Literature faculty and graduate students in the MFA Program in Writing. The readings are followed by in-depth question and answer periods that center on craft and artistic practice. The New Writing Series is co-sponsored by the Department of Literature, the International House, and the UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. Recordings of New Writing Series readings, as well as its predecessor, the New Poetry Series, which dates back to 1972, are part of the Archive for New Poetry in UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. Join us on Wednesday, December 2nd from 5:00PM-7:00PM in the Great Hall for the New Writing Series. This event features readings from the UCSD Literature Department's PHD students: Ana Villalpando, Nilufar Karimi, Phuong Vuong, Traimaine Suubi, and Vyxz Vasquez. Please register for this event here! Speaker Information: Ana Villalpando is a transfronteriza researcher and artist born in Tijuana, Mexico. She holds a BA in Philosophy from the Autonomous University of Baja California, an MA in Education from California State University, Long Beach and is currently pursuing a PhD in Literatures in Spanish at University of California, San Diego. Her art has been exhibited at The Front, The Woo and Centro Cultural La Raza in San Diego, California; her poetry has been published by UCLA’s Párrafo magazine, Chilean magazine La Raza cómica, NYU's Esferas Journal and UTEP's Rio Grande Review. Phuong T. Vuong is a Vietnamese American poet and writer raised in Oakland, CA. She is a PhD candidate in the Literature Department at UCSD, where she researches Asian American feminist and queer texts’ approaches to history, refusal, and relations to land and water. Phuong is the author of two poetry collections, A Plucked Zither (Red Hen Press, 2023), which won the Benjamin Saltman Poetry Award 2021, and The House I Inherit (Finishing Line Press, 2019). Her poetry and essays have also been published in a range of literary journals. Nilufar Karimi is a poet, scholar, translator and educator. Her work thinks through the intersections of translation, environmental justice, disability, and the practices of medicine. She is the author of Nuclear Deal (Noemi Press, 2021) and Notes on Digging (Belladonna*Collaborative, 2022) Tramaine Suubi is a multilingual writer who was born in Kampala. Tramaine is a graduate of the Iowa Wirters' Workshop and the author of two full-length poetry collections. Vyxz Vasquez is a writer and educator from the Philippines. She released two books this year: One Time Big Time & other poems (University of the Philippines Press), which is her first full-length collection, and Pensionados from Tijuana-based small press ediciones caradura. Our events are FREE and open to the public!

record.title: PARA/normal Borders Conversation III: Cristina Rivera Garza + Fred Moten
record.description: Cristina Rivera Garza + Fred Moten Part III of the PARA/normal Borders Conversation Series Language is one of the many borders that shape our lives. It carries histories, preserves memory, and creates new possibilities for connection across difference. Writers Cristina Rivera Garza and Fred Moten will both read from their work and then engage in a conversation about translation, poetry, and collective study, examining how literature moves across linguistic, cultural, and institutional boundaries. Together, they explore how literary practice can confront history, imagine new futures, and expand the possibilities of shared knowledge. PARA/normal Borders is the 2026–27 edition of the MexiCali Biennial, a multidisciplinary exhibition and public humanities initiative exploring the borderlands as a space where visible and invisible histories converge. Rather than treating the border solely as a geopolitical boundary, the project approaches it as a cultural, psychological, ecological, and technological condition that shapes contemporary life. Inspired by the concept of the borderlands as a “thin place,” PARA/normal Borders considers how migration, language, memory, Indigenous knowledge, media, surveillance, and speculative futures intersect across the California–Mexico border region. Through exhibitions, performances, publications, research initiatives, and public conversations, the Biennial invites artists, writers, scholars, and communities to examine the many ways borders continue to influence how we remember, imagine, and inhabit the world. The PARA/normal Borders Conversation Series brings together MacArthur Fellows whose work expands our understanding of borders across literature, film, visual art, music, and critical scholarship. This program is co-presented by MacArthur Foundation, the MexiCali Biennial and the University of California, San Diego Department of Literature’s New Writing Series, in partnership with the University of California, San Diego Department of Visual Arts and the Archive for New Poetry, and GalleryQI.

record.title: Exploring Connection: Books on Friendship, Community & Belonging
record.description: Social connection matters for your health and well-being. Strong social ties may protect against illness, ease stress, and even add years to your life – while isolation and loneliness raise the risk of illness, according to the U.S. Surgeon General’s Advisory on Social Connection. This November, visit the Meet Spot in Geisel Library's lobby during building open hours to explore books on friendship, community, and belonging. Our display features practical guides on building connection, research on why it matters, and stories that explore what belonging feels like. See the full book list. We developed this display as part of the San Diego Circuit Belonging & Mental Wellness Campaign, a collaborative effort by libraries across San Diego County to foster community and support mental health. Students, faculty, and staff can use Circuit to request additional books from participating libraries, including bestsellers, popular fiction, and other titles not in our collection. Visit lib.ucsd.edu/circuit for details.

record.title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
record.description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. This exhibit highlights five titles that mark milestones in the growth of the UC San Diego Library’s physical collections. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. record.title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
record.description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.
